883.title: The field of Siffin
883.hook: Ali's army and Mu'awiyah's meet, Qur'ans are raised on spears, and arbitration is agreed
883.howItsDone: Muslims study Siffin as part of the history of the fitnah; Sunni teaching holds Ali was in the right while counting Mu'awiyah a companion, and Shia Muslims regard Mu'awiyah as a rebel against the rightful Imam.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Battle of the Camel, and a verse about two parties of believers. Your line was believers against believers. Did you honor someone you disagree with? Day eight hundred eighty-three.

Spears go up along a battle line, and on their points are not banners but pages. Pages of the Qur'an. The army holding them is Syrian, led by Mu'awiyah, the governor of Syria and a kinsman of Uthman. The army facing them is Ali's. They have fought for days on a plain near the Euphrates, and the histories say Ali's side was pressing hard. Then the pages rise, and a call goes across the field: let the Book of God judge between us. Every soldier on Ali's side now has to decide what those pages mean. Today, the place where this happened.
screen: `SPEARS GO UP.` → `PAGES, NOT BANNERS.` → `LET THE BOOK JUDGE.`

segments.voice: Mu'awiyah had refused to pledge to Ali until Uthman's killers were handed over. Ali held that Mu'awiyah must first accept his caliphate. Neither would move, and the armies met at Siffin. The raised pages, the histories say, were the idea of Amr ibn al-As, on Mu'awiyah's side. Was it a sincere call to the Qur'an, or a way to stop a losing fight? The sources leave room for both readings. Ali, reports say, suspected a stratagem. But soldiers in his own ranks would not fight against the raised pages, and they pressed him to accept. He agreed to arbitration: one man chosen by each side, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari for Ali, Amr ibn al-As for Mu'awiyah, to judge by the Qur'an and the Prophet's way. Bukhari preserves a voice from those days. Sahl ibn Hunayf, who was with Ali, tells his own side: suspect your own opinion. He reminds them of Hudaybiyyah, years before, when the Prophet accepted a truce that looked like a defeat, and Umar had objected, and the truce turned out to be an opening. The point he draws for them: a settlement can be right even when it feels like losing. How Muslims judge Siffin differs. In Sunni teaching, Ali was in the right and Mu'awiyah erred in his judgment, while Mu'awiyah is still counted a companion. Shia Muslims see Mu'awiyah as a rebel against the rightful Imam and read the pages as a trick. Either way, the picture stays: pages on the spears, and a battle stopped for words.
screen: `NEITHER WOULD MOVE.` · `AMR'S IDEA, THE HISTORIES SAY.` · `ONE JUDGE FROM EACH SIDE.` · `SUSPECT YOUR OWN OPINION.` · then, large: `PAGES ON THE SPEARS.`

segments.voice: The practice: agree to talk. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a standoff you're part of, where neither side will move first. Breathe in, and notice the voice that says talking now would be losing. Breathe out, and borrow Sahl's words for a moment: suspect your own opinion. Not drop it. Just hold it a little more loosely. Then think of one small offer to talk you could make, a message, a time, a neutral place. If you pray, you can ask for an open heart in it. The bell holds the time.
Siffin, the plain near the Euphrates: where Ali's army and Mu'awiyah's met, pages of the Qur'an were raised on spears, and arbitration was agreed. Today's word.

Your line: pages on the spears. Today, when someone quotes a rule or a text at you mid-argument, ask yourself honestly whether it's a call to agree or a way to win, and then whether the same is true of you. Day eight hundred eighty-three.

884.title: The Kharijites
884.hook: a group rejects the arbitration, declares others unbelievers, and fights Ali
884.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often use the Kharijites as a warning against takfir, declaring other Muslims unbelievers, and cite the hadith that the charge returns to one of the two.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Siffin: the fighting stopped and two judges were chosen. Your line was pages on the spears. Did you catch a text being used to win rather than to agree? Day eight hundred eighty-four.

No judgment but God's. In Arabic, la hukma illa lillah. On their face, those are words nobody in Ali's camp would argue with. But a group of his own soldiers begins shouting them at him. They say: you let men judge between you and Mu'awiyah, and judgment belongs to God alone. Some of them, the histories note, were among those who had pushed him to accept the talks in the first place. Now they walk out of his camp and set up their own. Today's word is the name the walkout earned them.
screen: `NO JUDGMENT BUT GOD'S.` → `SHOUTED AT ALI.` → `THEY WALK OUT.`

segments.voice: Kharijites, in Arabic khawarij: those who went out. Ali's answer to their slogan is kept in Sahih Muslim: a word of truth, by which falsehood is intended. The words were true. What they were being used for was not. And what were they used for? The Kharijites came to hold that anyone who accepted the arbitration had committed a grave sin, and that such a person was no longer a believer. Ali, they said, had left Islam. So had anyone who stood with him. Once you've declared someone an unbeliever, the histories show how quickly the next step comes. Reports say they killed Muslims on the road who would not condemn Ali. Ali first sent his cousin Ibn Abbas to reason with them, and the reports say some came back. The rest he fought at Nahrawan. The Prophet had warned about this move long before. Bukhari records him saying that if a person calls his brother an unbeliever, the word returns to one of the two of them. In other words, the charge is dangerous enough that it can land on the one who makes it. Bukhari and Muslim also report the Prophet describing people who would recite the Qur'an but whose recitation would not go past their throats, and Muslim's collection sets that warning beside Ali and the men he faced. A note of fairness: Ibadi Muslims, in Oman and elsewhere, trace part of their history to early dissenters of this time, but they reject the name Kharijite and the extremes it stands for. The lesson the tradition draws is about a single move: declaring. Your line: not our place to declare.
screen: `KHAWARIJ: THOSE WHO WENT OUT.` · `A WORD OF TRUTH, FOR FALSEHOOD.` · `THE WORD RETURNS TO ONE OF THE TWO.` · `IBADIS REJECT THE NAME.` · then, large: `NOT OUR PLACE TO DECLARE.`

segments.voice: The practice: notice the danger of calling others unbelievers, or anything like it. Settle, and breathe. Think of the labels you reach for to put someone outside: fake, sellout, not a real one, not one of us. Breathe in, and find one person you've quietly placed outside the circle. Breathe out, and hand the verdict back. You can still disagree with them completely. You just don't sign the declaration. If you pray, you can leave the judgment with God. The bell holds the time.
The Kharijites. Those who went out: soldiers who left Ali over the arbitration, declared other Muslims unbelievers, and fought him at Nahrawan. Today's word.
Your line: not our place to declare. Today, when you hear yourself about to say someone isn't a real anything, stop at the label and talk about the action instead. Day eight hundred eighty-four.

885.title: The shield and the judge
885.hook: a well-known report: Ali loses a case against a Christian over a shield, because he has no witness, and the man becomes Muslim
885.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often tell the report of Ali and the judge Shurayh when teaching that rulers stand equal before the law, while noting that hadith scholars have questioned its chain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kharijites, who went out and declared others unbelievers. Your line was not our place to declare. Did you stop at a label and talk about the action instead? Day eight hundred eighty-five.

A stall in the market of Kufa, and on it, for sale, a piece of battle gear. A man walking past stops. He knows it. It's his. It went missing, and here it is, in the hands of a Christian trader. The man walking past is Ali, commander of the faithful, ruler of the Muslims. He could have it taken with a word. Instead, the story goes, he says: let's go to the judge. This is a well-known report, and it is worth hearing carefully, because it is more about the judge than the shield. Today, a courtroom.
screen: `A STALL IN KUFA.` → `THAT'S MINE.` → `LET'S GO TO THE JUDGE.`

segments.voice: The judge is Shurayh, appointed by the caliphs. The caliph walks in as an ordinary party to a case, and in some tellings he gently objects when Shurayh shows him more respect than the other man. The claim is simple. Ali says: it's mine. The trader says: it's mine, and it's in my hand. Shurayh turns to Ali. Do you have witnesses? Ali brings his son Hasan, and in some tellings his servant Qanbar too. And the judge says, in the telling, that he will not accept a son's testimony for his father. Ali has no further proof. So Shurayh rules for the trader. The caliph lost the case, before his own judge, in his own city. The trader walks out with the gear, and then turns back. The ruler of the Muslims, he says, brought me before his own judge, and the judge ruled against him. He says the gear really is Ali's, that it fell from his camel on the road, and he declares himself a Muslim. In the story, Ali gives it to him as a gift. Now the careful part. The report is found in later collections, such as al-Bayhaqi's, and hadith scholars have questioned the strength of its chain. Some tellings make the trader a Jewish man rather than a Christian. And the gear is often a coat of mail rather than a shield. So it is best heard as a report the tradition loves, not a sealed record. What it keeps alive is a command the Qur'an gives: when you judge between people, judge with justice. Shurayh did, even with the caliph standing before him. A ruler who loses fairly in his own court.
screen: `THE CALIPH AS AN ORDINARY PARTY.` · `NO SON'S TESTIMONY FOR HIS FATHER.` · `THE TRADER TURNS BACK.` · `A LOVED REPORT, A QUESTIONED CHAIN.` · then, large: `THE CALIPH LOST THE CASE.`

segments.voice: The practice: accept a fair ruling against you. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a time recently when a decision went against you, and the process was fair. A referee's call. A review at work. A vote in the family. A friend who said, honestly, you were wrong there. Breathe in, and notice whether any part of you is still arguing the case. Breathe out, and let the ruling stand. You can be sure you were right and still honor a fair process. If you pray, you can ask for a just heart. The bell holds the time.
Qadi, a judge: Shurayh, before whom Ali, as caliph, lost a case for lack of a witness, and the other man, moved by the fairness, became Muslim. Today's word.

Your line: the caliph lost the case. Today, if you hold any power over someone, a parent, a boss, a team lead, let one decision go to them on its merits, even when you could overrule it. Day eight hundred eighty-five.

886.title: Ali's death
886.hook: Ali is struck in the mosque at Kufa during Ramadan, and asks that his killer be treated fairly (reported)
886.howItsDone: Shia Muslims mourn Ali's wounding and death on nights of Ramadan with prayer and gatherings and visit his shrine at Najaf; Sunni Muslims honor him as the fourth rightly guided caliph and retell his instructions about his killer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shield and the qadi: Ali took his claim to court and lost for lack of a witness. Your line was the caliph lost the case. Did you let a fair decision go against you? Day eight hundred eighty-six.

A man named Ibn Muljam is in the mosque at Kufa, and he has a sword. He is one of the Kharijites, the ones who declared Ali an unbeliever for agreeing to talk at Siffin. It is Ramadan, still dark, and people are coming in for the dawn prayer. Ali, the caliph, is among them. Umar fell at this same hour, in Medina. Now, at the dawn prayer in Kufa, Ibn Muljam strikes Ali on the head. The wound is deep. Ali is carried home. What he says in the days that follow is the reason this lesson exists.
screen: `DARK, AND RAMADAN.` → `A SWORD AT DAWN PRAYER.` → `CARRIED HOME.`

segments.voice: Reports say that when he was struck, Ali said: by the Lord of the Ka'bah, I have won. Shia and Sunni sources both carry versions of this. A man struck down at prayer, in the month of fasting, counting it as victory. Then come his instructions about the man who did it. The histories, and the letter of counsel to his sons Hasan and Husayn kept in Nahj al-Balagha, give them like this. Keep him well. Feed him, and give him somewhere decent to stay. If I live, I will decide what to do with him; I may forgive him. If I die, then one blow for one blow. Do not kill anyone else on my account. And do not mutilate him, because the Prophet, peace be upon him, forbade mutilation, even of a rabid dog. Set that against the times. A city in turmoil. A ruler killed by a man who called him an unbeliever. And the dying man's worry is that his own side might go too far. No mob. No revenge on a whole tribe. Only what the law allows, and nothing beyond it, with forgiveness left open. That is your line: fair to his killer. Ali died of the wound soon after. Sunni Muslims honor him as the fourth of the rightly guided caliphs. Shia Muslims mourn him as the first Imam, and they observe the nights of his wounding and his death in Ramadan with prayer and grief. His shrine at Najaf, in Iraq, is where Shia Muslims hold he is buried, and pilgrims go there. The fitnah was not over, but this is how Ali left it.
screen: `I HAVE WON, BY THE LORD OF THE KA'BAH.` · `FEED HIM. KEEP HIM WELL.` · `ONE BLOW FOR ONE BLOW, NO MORE.` · `MOURNED IN RAMADAN.` · then, large: `FAIR TO HIS KILLER.`

segments.voice: The practice: be fair even to an enemy. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who has wronged you, a real wrong, not a small one. Breathe in, and notice what you'd like to happen to them. Then ask the narrower question Ali asked: what would actually be fair? Not more. Breathe out, and let go of the part that goes beyond fair, the extra blow, the story told to everyone, the punishment of people around them. If you pray, you can leave the rest with God. The bell holds the time.

Ali's death. Struck at the dawn prayer in the mosque at Kufa in Ramadan by a Kharijite, he asked, the reports say, that his killer be kept well and treated within the law, and no further. Today's word.
Your line: fair to his killer. Today, when you talk about someone who has hurt you, say only what is true and fair, and leave out the extra. Day eight hundred eighty-six.

887.title: Hasan's peace
887.hook: Hasan makes a treaty with Mu'awiyah to stop the bloodshed, as the Prophet ﷺ foretold (Bukhari)
887.howItsDone: Muslims recall Hasan's treaty with Mu'awiyah through the hadith in Bukhari in which the Prophet calls Hasan a leader through whom God may make peace between two groups of Muslims; Shia Muslims honor Hasan as the second Imam.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ali's death: struck in the mosque at Kufa, and asking, the reports say, that his attacker be dealt with fairly. Your line was: fair to his killer. Who did you treat fairly when you didn't have to? Day eight hundred eighty-seven.

A boy sits beside his grandfather on the pulpit in Medina. The grandfather is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. He looks out at the people, then at the boy, then out at the people again, and says something about the boy's future. This son of mine is a sayyid, a leader, and perhaps through him God will make peace between two great groups of Muslims. Bukhari keeps the scene. The boy is Hasan, Ali's elder son. And years later, after his father's death, Hasan stands at the head of an army facing another army. Today: Hasan's peace.
screen: `A BOY ON THE PULPIT.` → `THIS SON OF MINE IS A LEADER.` → `TWO GREAT GROUPS.`

segments.voice: Bukhari keeps the second scene too, in the words of a later narrator, al-Hasan al-Basri. Hasan leads armies he describes as like mountains. Facing him are the forces of Mu'awiyah, the governor of Syria. One of Mu'awiyah's advisers says these armies will not turn back until each has destroyed the other. And Mu'awiyah asks a question worth hearing: if these kill those and those kill these, who will be left to look after the people, their families, their affairs? So he sends two men to Hasan, to talk. Hasan listens. And Hasan agrees to step aside and make peace. The histories report conditions in the treaty, and they differ about the details, so the details are best left to them. What Bukhari records is the outcome, and the narrator ties it straight back to the pulpit: the Prophet had said that through this son, God might make peace between two great groups. The two groups are not believers and enemies. Both are Muslims. That is what makes the moment heavy. After the Camel and Siffin, believers against believers, a grandson of the Prophet chooses to give up a claim rather than add to the graves. Muslims remember this differently, and fairly. Shia Muslims honor Hasan as the second Imam, and read the treaty as a wise and costly choice made to protect the believers when war would only have destroyed them. Sunni Muslims honor Hasan as a member of the Prophet's household and a companion, and point to this hadith as the Prophet's own praise of what he did. Tradition calls that year the year of unity. And so the part of the story that began with Ali as caliph ends here, not on a battlefield, but with a treaty.
screen: `ARMIES LIKE MOUNTAINS.` · `WHO WILL BE LEFT TO CARE FOR THE PEOPLE?` · `HASAN STEPS ASIDE.` · `BOTH GROUPS ARE MUSLIMS.` · then, large: `PEACE BETWEEN TWO GROUPS.`

segments.voice: The practice: give up a claim for peace. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one standing argument in your life. A sibling, a coworker, a neighbor, a group chat. Something where you are, quite possibly, right. Breathe in, and ask Mu'awiyah's question: if this goes on, who is left to look after the people in between? The kids, the team, the friends caught in the middle. Breathe out. You don't have to surrender anything yet. Just hold the claim in an open hand, and see what it would cost to set it down. The bell holds the time.
Hasan's peace. A grandson of the Prophet who could have fought, and instead stepped aside so two groups of Muslims would stop killing each other. Today's word.
Your line: peace between two groups. Today, in one disagreement, let go of being proven right, and notice what the other person does next. Day eight hundred eighty-seven.

888.title: Rule from Damascus
888.hook: Mu'awiyah rules from Damascus, and the caliphate becomes a dynasty
888.howItsDone: Muslims remember the move of the caliphate to Damascus under Mu'awiyah as the start of the Umayyad dynasty; Sunni Muslims honor him as a companion while often criticizing the hereditary turn, and Shia Muslims remember him as Ali's opponent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hasan's peace: a grandson of the Prophet who stepped aside rather than add to the graves. Your line was: peace between two groups. What claim did you hold in an open hand? Day eight hundred eighty-eight.

Medina had been the center. The Prophet, peace be upon him, was buried there. Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman had led from there. Ali had moved to Kufa, in Iraq. And now the seat of the Muslim community moves again, north, to an old city: Damascus. The man who rules from there is Mu'awiyah, who had governed Syria under the earlier caliphs. With him, the question that had split the believers since the day after the Prophet's death takes a new shape. Not only who should lead, but how leadership passes on. Today: rule from Damascus.
screen: `MEDINA, THEN KUFA.` → `NOW DAMASCUS.` → `HOW DOES LEADERSHIP PASS ON?`

segments.voice: Up to now, each caliph had come to office a different way. Abu Bakr by a pledge in a meeting hall. Umar named by Abu Bakr. Uthman chosen by a council. Ali by a pledge in the mosque, in a crisis. None was a son taking over from a father. The histories report that in his later years Mu'awiyah asked the people to pledge loyalty, in advance, to his son Yazid. Some refused. Several sons of the great companions in Medina are reported among them, and so is Husayn. But the pledge was taken, and when Mu'awiyah died, Yazid ruled. The rule of one family, the Umayyads, had begun, and it would pass from father to son, or cousin to cousin, for generations. Muslims had words for this change. A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi says that the caliphate of prophethood would last thirty years, and after it God would give kingship to whom He wills. In Arabic, the word for that kingship is mulk. Some scholars read that hadith against this very moment. Sunni and Shia Muslims see Mu'awiyah differently, and both views deserve to be heard as their holders hold them. Sunni Muslims count him a companion of the Prophet, and Sunni teaching gives him the respect owed to companions, while some Sunni scholars are frank that turning the caliphate into an inheritance was a change for the worse. Shia Muslims see him as the man who fought Ali, the rightful Imam, and who set the stage for the tragedy that came next. Either way, the shape of power changed in Damascus. A community that had chosen its leaders now inherited them.
screen: `FOUR CALIPHS, FOUR WAYS IN.` · `A PLEDGE FOR YAZID, IN ADVANCE.` · `CALIPHATE, THEN KINGSHIP.` · `SUNNI AND SHIA SEE HIM DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `A DYNASTY BEGINS.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about power passing in families. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you were handed down that you didn't choose. A family business, a role, a name, a way of doing things, a grudge. Breathe in. Ask which parts of it you received because they were right, and which only because they were yours. Breathe out. Then think of something you will hand on to someone else, a job, a home, a habit, and ask how it could be passed on fairly, not just kept in the family. The bell holds the time.
Mulk, kingship: the hadith's word for the rule God gives after the caliphate of prophethood, the moment Mu'awiyah's rule began to pass from father to son. Today's word.

889.title: Husayn refuses
889.hook: Husayn refuses to give his pledge to Yazid and sets out for Kufa with his family
889.howItsDone: Muslims retell Husayn's refusal to pledge to Yazid as the opening of the Karbala story; Shia Muslims honor him as the third Imam, and Sunni and Shia Muslims alike keep the Prophet's words, Husayn is from me and I am from Husayn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mulk, rule from Damascus: Mu'awiyah asks for a pledge to his son in advance, and a community that chose its leaders begins to inherit them. Your line was: a dynasty begins. What did you notice being handed on? Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

A messenger knocks in Medina, at night. The governor wants to see Husayn, now. Mu'awiyah is dead, the histories say, and his son Yazid has written: take the pledge from Husayn, and do not let him put it off. Husayn is the younger son of Ali and Fatima, a grandson of the Prophet, peace be upon him. He goes to the governor. He listens. And he asks for time: a pledge like this, he says, should be made in public, before the people, not in a room at night. Then he leaves, and before long he leaves Medina altogether. Today: Husayn refuses.
screen: `A KNOCK AT NIGHT.` → `TAKE THE PLEDGE FROM HUSAYN.` → `NOT IN A ROOM AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: A pledge, a bay'ah, was not a vote. It was a handclasp that bound you to obey. Giving it to Yazid would have meant saying yes to the new shape of power. Husayn would not give it. The histories follow him to Mecca, where he stays near the Kaaba. Then letters start to arrive from Kufa, his father's old city, many letters, the reports say, inviting him to come and lead them. He sends his cousin, Muslim ibn Aqil, ahead to see if the welcome is real. And then, against the advice of relatives and friends who are reported to have begged him to stay, he sets out across the desert. Not with an army. With his family: his sisters, his wives, his children, his brothers, a small circle of companions. Why? Muslims have answered that in different ways. Shia Muslims honor Husayn as the third Imam, and hear in his refusal a stand for the religion itself: that a ruler who did not live by it could not be given the believers' hands. Sunni Muslims honor him as a beloved grandson of the Prophet who refused injustice, though some Sunni scholars held that he should have stayed. Tirmidhi keeps a hadith in which the Prophet says, Husayn is from me, and I am from Husayn. And this is the end of a week. It began at Siffin, with pages on the spears; then the Kharijites, a caliph losing a case over a shield, Ali's death, Hasan's peace, and rule from Damascus. It ends with a man on a road, who would not pledge.
screen: `A PLEDGE WAS A HANDCLASP.` · `LETTERS FROM KUFA.` · `NOT AN ARMY: A FAMILY.` · `HUSAYN IS FROM ME.` · then, large: `HE WOULD NOT PLEDGE.`

segments.voice: The practice: refuse one wrong thing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you've been going along with that you know isn't right. A joke at someone's expense. A shortcut at work. A silence when someone is being treated badly. Breathe in. Notice how small the yes has become, how easy. Breathe out. Picture yourself saying no, plainly and without drama, the way Husayn answered the governor: calm, polite, and unmoved. Choose the words you would use. The bell holds the time.
